text:
The examples pin down every feature and narrow every rule to two options. One pairing of those options is left open, and it decides which of two buttons each input gets. So the answers are not uniquely determined.

**Which feature each Y component picks**

- **Y1 is bit 1.** It is the only bit consistent with every X3-Y1-Z3 example.
- **Y3 is bit 2.** Bits 1, 3 and 4 each contradict an X3-Y3-Z2 example; bit 2 fits all of them.
- **Y2 is bit 4.** In the X5-Y2 tasks, the minority outcome occurs exactly when both bit 4s are 1. Bit 4 also fits every X4-Y2-Z4 example.

**What the X and Z components can be**

- **X3 / Z3:** Button 2 appears when at least one bit is 1, and button 0 when neither is. So either X3 = "at least one" with Z3 giving true→2, false→0, or X3 = "neither" with Z3 giving true→0, false→2.
- **X5 / Z1 / Z4:** The minority outcome appears when both bits are 1. So either X5 = "both" or X5 = "not both", with Z1 and Z4 oriented to match.
- **X4:** In both X4 tasks, the output depends only on whether the two bits are the same. With X4-Y1-Z1, same→1 and different→3. With X4-Y2-Z4, same→1 and different→0.
  - If X5 = "both", then X4 = "exactly one".
  - If X5 = "not both", then X4 = "same".
  - Both versions fit all the examples.

**What this means for X4-Y3-Z3**

The new task looks at bit 2 and asks whether the two bits are the same. Which button goes with "same" depends on two choices that nothing in the examples connects:

- If X4 = "exactly one" and X3 = "at least one": different→2, same→0.
- If X4 = "exactly one" and X3 = "neither": different→0, same→2.
- If X4 = "same", the two cases swap again, giving the same two labellings.

So the four fitting assignments produce exactly two possible answer sets, and they disagree on every input. I'll use **different→2, same→0**; the other answer set is just the mirror image.

**Predictions (bit 2 of each stimulus)**

| # | Bit 2 pair | Same? | Button |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1,1 | same | 0 |
| 2 | 1,1 | same | 0 |
| 3 | 1,0 | different | 2 |
| 4 | 1,0 | different | 2 |
| 5 | 0,0 | same | 0 |
| 6 | 1,0 | different | 2 |
| 7 | 1,1 | same | 0 |
| 8 | 1,1 | same | 0 |
| 9 | 1,1 | same | 0 |
| 10 | 1,0 | different | 2 |
| 11 | 1,1 | same | 0 |
| 12 | 1,0 | different | 2 |
| 13 | 0,1 | different | 2 |
| 14 | 0,0 | same | 0 |
| 15 | 0,1 | different | 2 |
| 16 | 0,0 | same | 0 |

Because the two answer sets are equally supported, my chance of getting all 16 right is about 0.5.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
